questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When a MOTOR nerve is electrically stimulated, why does only the downward-travelling (efferent) impulse produce a muscle contraction, while the upward-travelling impulse has no motor effect?

options.A: The upward-travelling impulse is unable to pass the first synapse, since it is travelling in the wrong (antidromic) direction
options.B: The upward-travelling impulse travels faster and arrives too early to have any effect
options.C: Motor nerves cannot conduct impulses in more than one direction under any circumstance
options.D: Only the upward-travelling impulse reaches the muscle

questions.explanation: Stimulating a nerve fibre initiates impulses travelling simultaneously in both directions from the stimulation point. For a motor nerve, the upward (antidromic) impulse cannot pass the first synapse it encounters travelling the 'wrong' way, so it has no effect, while the downward (orthodromic) impulse reaches the muscle normally and causes contraction.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Nerve Stimulation

questions.question: Although prolactin levels are high throughout pregnancy, actual milk secretion does not begin until around the 3rd-4th postpartum day. What explains this delay?

options.A: Prolactin has no role in milk secretion at all
options.B: High circulating estrogen and progesterone during pregnancy make breast tissue unresponsive to prolactin; their withdrawal after delivery allows prolactin to act
options.C: The breasts are not anatomically ready until several days after birth
options.D: Oxytocin blocks prolactin receptors until labour is complete

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, the high circulating levels of estrogen and progesterone keep the fully-developed mammary glands unresponsive to prolactin, holding milk secretion in abeyance despite high prolactin levels. Once these steroids fall sharply after delivery, prolactin is free to begin its secretory (lactogenic) action.

questions.question: Because of accommodation, which type of current change is MORE effective at initiating a nerve impulse: a sudden change, or a gradual one?

options.A: A sudden change in current is more effective than a gradual one
options.B: A gradual change is always more effective
options.C: Both are exactly equally effective in all cases
options.D: Neither a sudden nor gradual change can ever initiate an impulse

questions.explanation: Because the nerve accommodates (adapts) to slowly changing conditions, a current that rises or falls suddenly is more effective at initiating an impulse than one that changes gradually, since gradual change gives the nerve time to accommodate before the threshold is reached.

questions.question: A drug that reacts with an enzyme's catalytic site so strongly (via a covalent bond or very high affinity) that the normal substrate cannot displace it produces which kinetic pattern?

options.A: kM unchanged, Vmax unchanged (no real inhibition)
options.C: kM increased and Vmax reduced — a non-equilibrium type of competitive inhibition
options.D: Only Vmax changes while kM decreases proportionally

questions.explanation: Classical competitive inhibition (equilibrium type) raises kM but leaves Vmax unchanged, since enough substrate can still out-compete the inhibitor. But when the inhibitor binds essentially irreversibly at the same catalytic site (e.g. organophosphates on cholinesterase, or methotrexate's very high affinity for dihydrofolate reductase), substrate can no longer displace it — this non-equilibrium type raises kM AND reduces Vmax.

questions.question: After a fracture of both the radius and ulna shafts, why must cross-union (bony union between the two bones) be specifically prevented during healing?

options.C: Cross-union only affects elbow flexion, not the hand

questions.question: Edman's reagent (phenylisothiocyanate) is used in protein sequencing chiefly because it allows:

options.A: Complete hydrolysis of the protein into free amino acids only
options.B: Selective labelling and removal of the N-terminal amino acid as a PTH-derivative, leaving the rest of the polypeptide intact for repeated cycles
options.C: Cleavage of the protein only at cysteine residues
options.D: Permanent, irreversible denaturation of all peptide bonds

questions.explanation: Unlike Sanger's reagent (which labels and then requires full hydrolysis, destroying the polypeptide), Edman's reagent selectively removes and identifies the N-terminal amino acid as a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) derivative while leaving the remaining polypeptide intact — allowing the process to be repeated cycle after cycle to read the sequence progressively.

questions.question: During a maximum-effort CONCENTRIC muscle contraction, what happens to the force a muscle can generate as the velocity of shortening increases?

questions.question: Plasmodium falciparum causes markedly more severe (malignant) malaria than the other three plasmodial species mainly because:

options.A: It has an exo-erythrocytic stage that the others lack
options.B: It only infects the liver, never red blood cells
options.C: It parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell multiple times, and makes parasitised red cells sticky, causing capillary obstruction in deep organs
options.D: It is transmitted by a different mosquito genus entirely

questions.explanation: Unlike the other plasmodial species (which parasitise only juvenile red cells and lack these features), P. falciparum parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell with more than one parasite, and makes infected red cells sticky — causing capillary obstruction (e.g. in the brain, producing cerebral malaria) that accounts for its exceptional virulence. It also notably lacks an exo-erythrocytic stage, but that is not the source of its severity.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Population inversion in laser physics refers to a state in which:

options.A: More electrons are in the ground state than in the excited state
options.B: The medium is at absolute zero
options.C: More electrons are in an excited (metastable) state than in the ground state
options.D: All electrons are removed from the atom

questions.explanation: Population inversion is required for stimulated emission to exceed absorption and thereby amplify light.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: 'Physical dependence' on a drug is best defined as:

options.A: Simply enjoying the effects of a drug with no physiological consequence of stopping it
options.B: An altered physiological state (neuroadaptation) requiring the continued presence of the drug to maintain equilibrium, such that stopping it produces a characteristic withdrawal syndrome
options.C: A purely psychological craving with no biological basis whatsoever
options.D: A condition seen only with stimulant drugs like cocaine and amphetamines

questions.explanation: Physical dependence is an altered physiological state produced by repeated drug administration, requiring the drug's continued presence to maintain equilibrium ('neuroadaptation'); stopping the drug produces a characteristic withdrawal syndrome. Drugs like opioids, barbiturates, alcohol, and benzodiazepines produce physical dependence, while stimulants like amphetamines and cocaine produce little or none, despite being highly reinforcing.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: The maximum predicted heart rate in a healthy adult is commonly estimated as:
questions.explanation: A 40-year-old: 180 bpm. Moderate intensity is ~64–76% of HRmax.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Tetanospasmin acts by blocking release of:

options.D: Inhibitory neurotransmitters (glycine and GABA) in the spinal cord

questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology; Ananthanarayan & Paniker, Textbook of Microbiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: If a patient with SCI on a tilt table becomes dizzy and nauseated, the most appropriate immediate action is to:

options.A: Leave the patient and call a colleague
options.C: Lower the tilt table (or recline the chair) and monitor vital signs

questions.explanation: Pooling of blood in the lower limbs due to loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone; use abdominal binders and stockings and increase angles gradually.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: A confounding factor is one that:

options.B: Lies on the causal pathway only
options.C: Is not associated with the outcome
options.D: Is associated with both the exposure and the outcome and distorts their observed relationship

questions.explanation: Control by randomisation, restriction, matching or adjustment.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine; WHO/ICF and CBR guidelines; standard biostatistics/research methodology texts (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 6 Research and Analysis)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Why do medium-frequency currents pass through the skin more comfortably than low-frequency currents?

options.B: Skin capacitive reactance falls as frequency rises, so skin impedance is lower
options.C: They are not conducted by nerves at all
options.D: Skin resistance rises as frequency rises

questions.explanation: Skin behaves partly as a capacitor. Capacitive reactance = 1/(2πfC), so at higher frequencies the impedance is lower and more current penetrates with less discomfort at the skin.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The Neer and Hawkins–Kennedy tests are used to detect:
questions.explanation: Passive forced flexion (Neer) or flexion with medial rotation at 90° (Hawkins) squeezes the supraspinatus against the coracoacromial arch.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: In the first week postpartum, there is a secondary increase in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and platelets. What clinical risk does this hypercoagulable state primarily raise?
questions.explanation: The secondary rise in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and platelet count (with increased platelet adhesiveness) during the first postpartum week increases the risk of thrombosis — one reason early ambulation and postpartum exercise are actively encouraged, since enhanced fibrinolytic activity in the first few days acts as a partial protective counter-mechanism.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: During full elevation of the arm the clavicle:

options.D: Rotates posteriorly about its long axis by about 30–50°

questions.explanation: Posterior rotation of the clavicle allows the scapula to upwardly rotate and permits complete elevation.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Neumann, Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System; Daniels & Worthingham (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 3 Biomechanics)
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The Y-BOCS, a widely used clinical scale for OCD, stands for and is used to:

options.A: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale — elicit symptoms and rate severity of OCD
options.B: Young-Beck Obsessive Cognition Scale — diagnose depression only
options.C: Yale Behavioural Outcome Classification System — used only in research, never clinically
options.D: A scale exclusively for measuring anxiety, unrelated to OCD

questions.explanation: Y-BOCS stands for the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale, one of the most useful clinical tools for eliciting the range of obsessive and compulsive symptoms present and rating the overall severity of OCD.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Rigor mortis occurs because of:

options.A: Lack of ATP, preventing detachment of myosin heads from actin

questions.explanation: ATP is needed for cross-bridge detachment.
questions.sourceBook: A.K. Jain, Textbook of Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Which treatment is inappropriate during an acute flare of rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation calls for rest, gentle range of motion and pain relief; stretching/mobilisation aggravates synovitis.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase) for ischaemic stroke should be started within:
questions.explanation: Haemorrhage must be excluded first with CT.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference); standard internal medicine texts
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Chorea, dementia and an autosomal dominant inheritance are features of:
questions.explanation: Degeneration of the caudate nucleus; CAG repeat expansion on chromosome 4.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Which muscle acts as the prime mover in the initial 0–15° of shoulder abduction?
questions.explanation: Supraspinatus initiates abduction (0–15°), the middle deltoid is the main abductor from 15–90°, then trapezius and serratus anterior rotate the scapula for elevation above 90°.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: In normal pregnancy, exercise should be avoided in the supine position after the first trimester because of:

options.A: Risk of pelvic girdle pain only
options.D: Compression of the inferior vena cava reducing venous return

questions.explanation: The supine hypotensive syndrome causes dizziness and reduced uteroplacental blood flow; use left lateral tilt.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: In periodized training, the 'competition' phase is generally characterized by:

options.A: Lower loads and the highest number of repetitions and sets
options.B: Higher loads (peaking just prior to competition), with fewer exercises per session and reduced volume compared to the preparation phase
options.D: Only aerobic exercise, no resistance training

questions.explanation: In periodized training, the competition phase uses higher loads peaking just before competition, along with fewer exercises per session and decreased repetitions/sets compared to the earlier preparation phase, which uses lower loads and higher volume.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Periodization and Variation of Training
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The physiological basis of hold-relax stretching is:

options.D: Autogenic inhibition via Golgi tendon organs after an isometric contraction

questions.explanation: A maximal isometric contraction of the shortened muscle stimulates GTOs, followed by relaxation and a deeper stretch.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques; Dena Gardiner, Principles of Exercise Therapy; Tidy's Physiotherapy (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Which of the following is a tumour-suppressor gene?
questions.explanation: p53 is the ‘guardian of the genome’; mutated in over 50% of human cancers.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology; Ananthanarayan & Paniker, Textbook of Microbiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: A hallmark intellectual deficit seen after prefrontal-lobe damage, distinct from a general drop in IQ (which is often unaffected), is:

options.A: Complete loss of the ability to speak
options.B: Difficulty planning and sequencing actions, plus perseveration (continuing a behaviour even when the situation demands a new response)
options.D: Immediate loss of all long-term memories formed before the injury

questions.explanation: While standard IQ tests are often little affected by prefrontal damage, patients show subtle but characteristic deficits: difficulty planning a sequence of actions, and perseveration — a tendency to keep behaving the same way even when circumstances call for a different response.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Frontal-Lobe Association Cortex
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Which aquatic activity is MOST effective in reducing tone in a patient with spasticity?

options.C: Slow, passive movements with the patient floating supported in warm water

questions.explanation: Warm water, buoyancy and slow rhythmic movements relax muscles; speed and cold increase tone.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques; Dena Gardiner, Principles of Exercise Therapy; Tidy's Physiotherapy (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: The normal arterial PaO2 in a healthy adult breathing room air is approximately:
questions.explanation: PaO2 <60 mmHg (8 kPa) defines type 1 respiratory failure; normal PaCO2 is 35–45 mmHg.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: The most important complication of an intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck is:
questions.explanation: The retinacular vessels (from the medial circumflex femoral artery) are disrupted.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 4 Orthopedics)
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Maximum coronary blood flow to the left ventricle occurs during:
questions.explanation: During systole intramyocardial pressure compresses the coronary vessels.
questions.sourceBook: A.K. Jain, Textbook of Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Post-operative atelectasis is MOST effectively prevented by:

options.B: Early mobilisation, deep breathing exercises and incentive spirometry

questions.explanation: Reduced lung volumes after anaesthesia and pain contribute; early ambulation and deep breathing restore functional residual capacity.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems; ACSM Guidelines; Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Curare paralyses skeletal muscle by:

options.A: Blocking calcium channels in the nerve terminal
options.C: Competitively blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor end plate

questions.explanation: Succinylcholine is a depolarising blocker; neostigmine reverses non-depolarising blocks.
questions.sourceBook: A.K. Jain, Textbook of Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: In supraspinatus tendinitis the typical painful arc during active abduction is:
questions.explanation: Pain between roughly 60° and 120° of abduction occurs as the tuberosity passes under the acromion; pain at the end of range suggests acromioclavicular pathology.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: The anaerobic (lactate) threshold is the exercise intensity at which:

options.D: Blood lactate begins to accumulate rapidly

questions.explanation: Training raises the threshold and improves endurance.
questions.sourceBook: A.K. Jain, Textbook of Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology (chapter-level reference)
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: To produce measurable separation of lumbar vertebrae, the traction force needs to exceed approximately:
questions.explanation: Because of the friction of the body on the couch and the strength of the lumbar ligaments, forces of roughly 50% of body weight or more are needed for lumbar separation; lower forces (about 25%) are used for comfort and initial treatment.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: A Bennett fracture is a:

options.B: Fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal
options.C: Fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal

questions.explanation: Intra-articular fracture-subluxation of the thumb CMC joint; the abductor pollicis longus displaces the shaft.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 4 Orthopedics)
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: The acute inflammatory stage of soft tissue healing typically lasts approximately how long, unless the insult is perpetuated?
questions.explanation: The acute inflammatory stage typically lasts 4 to 6 days unless the injury is continually aggravated. The subsequent subacute (proliferation/repair) stage usually lasts 10-17 days (up to 6 weeks in poorly vascularised tissues like tendons), and the chronic (maturation/remodeling) stage can last 6 months to 1 year.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Acute Stage
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: A 95% confidence interval for a mean means that:

options.A: If the study were repeated many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true population mean
options.C: The true mean has a 95% probability of being in any single interval after it has been calculated, with certainty
options.D: 95% of individual observations lie within it

questions.explanation: CI reflects precision of the estimate; if a CI for a difference excludes 0 (or ratio excludes 1) the result is significant at 5%.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine; WHO/ICF and CBR guidelines; standard biostatistics/research methodology texts (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 6 Research and Analysis)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: For a RISING (increasing) current applied over a superficial nerve, which electrode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse, and why is the active electrode typically connected to it?

options.A: The anode, because it requires less current overall
options.B: The cathode, because it produces contraction of innervated muscle with less current than is required at the anode
options.C: Neither electrode has any different effect
options.D: The anode always requires less current than the cathode

questions.explanation: For a rising current, the cathode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse than the anode. This is why the active electrode is conventionally connected to the cathode — it produces contraction of innervated muscle using less current than would be needed if the anode were used as the active electrode.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The capsular pattern of the knee joint is:
questions.explanation: Cyriax: knee = flexion > extension (e.g. 'gross loss of flexion, slight loss of extension'). Hip = flexion, abduction, medial rotation.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: A choke coil (inductor) in a circuit mainly:

options.A: Opposes rapid changes in current, allowing low-frequency/steady current but impeding high-frequency alternating current
options.B: Blocks direct current and passes only high frequencies

questions.explanation: An inductor's reactance rises with frequency (X = 2πfL), so it smooths current and attenuates high-frequency components.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: In PNF, the D1 flexion pattern of the upper limb consists of:

options.A: Shoulder flexion, adduction and lateral rotation with forearm supination and wrist flexion to the radial side
options.B: Shoulder extension and adduction with pronation
options.C: Shoulder extension, abduction and medial rotation
options.D: Shoulder flexion, abduction and lateral rotation

questions.explanation: D1 flexion moves across the face (similar to ‘protecting the head’); D2 flexion moves up and out (like drawing a sword).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Why can a meniscal injury sometimes present with little or no pain or swelling, making diagnosis more difficult?

options.A: The menisci are avascular and have no nerve supply on their inner two-thirds
options.B: The menisci are the most richly innervated structures in the knee
options.C: Meniscal tears always occur alongside complete ACL rupture, masking symptoms
options.D: Meniscal tissue regenerates immediately after injury

questions.explanation: The menisci are avascular and lack nerve supply on their inner two-thirds, meaning an injury confined to this region can produce little or no pain or swelling — one reason meniscal injury can be difficult to diagnose confidently without a thorough history and examination.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Meniscus Injury
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: The normal triangular relationship of the olecranon and the two epicondyles is lost in:
questions.explanation: In flexion the three bony points form an isosceles triangle; in a supracondylar fracture the relationship is maintained.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 4 Orthopedics)
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Intradiscal pressure of the lumbar spine is HIGHEST in:

options.A: Sitting while leaning forward with a load

questions.explanation: Nachemson: supine 25%, side-lying 75%, standing 100%, sitting 140%, sitting flexed with load 275%.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Neumann, Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System; Daniels & Worthingham (chapter-level reference; cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e, Ch. 3 Biomechanics)
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: In the Rancho Los Amigos Scale, level IV is characterised by:
questions.explanation: I no response; II generalised; III localised; IV confused-agitated; V confused-inappropriate; VI confused-appropriate; VII automatic-appropriate; VIII purposeful.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: A stress (fatigue) fracture is most common in the:

options.A: Metatarsals, tibia and neck of femur

questions.explanation: Repetitive loading, e.g. in runners and military recruits, produces fatigue fractures of the second/third metatarsal, tibia and femoral neck.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise; Maheshwari, Essential Orthopaedics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: BCR-ABL fusion; treated with imatinib.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference); standard internal medicine texts
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Clarke's sign and the McConnell test are both special tests associated with which condition?
questions.explanation: Clarke's sign and the McConnell test are both used in the assessment of patellofemoral syndrome (anterior knee pain related to patellar tracking/compression issues).
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Osler's nodes and Janeway lesions are features of:
questions.explanation: Osler's nodes are painful fingertip nodules; Janeway lesions are painless macules on the palms/soles; Roth spots in the retina.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine (chapter-level reference); standard internal medicine texts
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine is commonly associated with:

options.B: Tight hip flexors and erector spinae with weak abdominals and gluteals

questions.explanation: Lower crossed syndrome (Janda): anterior pelvic tilt from tight hip flexors/lumbar extensors and weak abdominals/gluteals.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment; Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise (facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills
